narrative: February 2026 is the inflection point of the dataset. In a single step the active count jumped by 52,427 codes — more than the previous three years of growth combined — with zero removals. Statistics Canada didn't prune anything; it bulk-loaded a large tranche of new delivery points, the signature of a feed re-sync rather than organic growth.

The additions land where you'd expect density and construction: dense urban cores — Toronto's M5W (586), Montréal's H3C (532, the Griffintown condo belt), Calgary's T2P (318) — and fast-growing commuter suburbs like Vaudreuil J7V (349), Surrey V3S (284) and Markham L3R (274). Ontario (17,701) and Quebec (11,641) dominate by volume, but New Brunswick's 5,231 is the outlier — far above its ~2% population share, split between Saint John (E2L) and Moncton (E1C) and a band of rural southern-NB routes (E4P/E4T/E4Z) that look like a long-overdue backfill.

Underneath sit 8,088 genuine changes — 6,392 boundary reassignments and 1,696 substantive renames, two-thirds of every real rename in the six-snapshot history. The bulk is municipal-designation realignment, and it runs in both directions. Greater Victoria pulled suburbs into the metro name — Langford → Victoria (1,392 codes), North Cowichan → Duncan (588) — while Quebec's Mauricie did the opposite, re-splitting the amalgamated city of Shawinigan back into its historical communities Grand-Mère (831) and Shawinigan-Sud (791). Windsor, QC absorbed Saint-Claude (1,358); Truro, NS took in Bible Hill (317).

The second story is noise: 75,318 “changes” that aren't. The feed repaired 301 distinct mis-encoded French names — and it's the biggest cities that dominate, because they appear on the most codes: Montréal alone accounts for 20,184, Québec 18,891, Trois-Rivières 5,879, Lévis 5,362. Mojibake like MontrÃ©al and Main-Ã-Dieu was normalised to Montreal and Main-A-Dieu. No place was renamed; only the bytes were fixed, so we quarantine the lot from every real total.

The two phenomena draw different maps. Additions favour Ontario and Quebec by raw volume, but genuine reorganisation tilts to Quebec (2,884 real) and British Columbia (2,092) — a reminder that where codes are added and where places are actually reshaped are not the same country.

added: The absence of any removals plus a step-change of this size points to a bulk delivery-area load — Statistics Canada re-syncing NAR to a fresh Canada Post address extract, not organic year-over-year growth (which has run 700–17,000/period elsewhere in the series).

The top FSAs read as two kinds of place: dense urban cores — Toronto M5W, Montréal H3C, Calgary T2P, Edmonton T5J, Winnipeg R3C — alongside high-growth commuter suburbs (Vaudreuil J7V, Surrey V3S, Markham L3R). New condo towers and greenfield subdivisions both generate blocks of fresh codes.

New Brunswick's 5,231 is the anomaly worth flagging: roughly triple its population share, split between the Saint John (E2L) and Moncton (E1C) urban areas and a band of rural southern-NB routes (E4P/E4T/E4Z) — the profile of a one-time backfill of routes NAR had been missing.
boundary: A postal code's municipal label changed while the location did not — the signature of municipal-boundary realignment. What's striking here is that it runs in both directions at once.

Consolidation dominates the west: Greater Victoria absorbed its suburbs' delivery names (Langford → Victoria, 1,392; North Cowichan → Duncan, 588), while Windsor, QC took in Saint-Claude (1,358) and Truro, NS absorbed Bible Hill (317).

The reverse happens in Quebec's Mauricie: codes previously labelled with the amalgamated city “Shawinigan” were re-split back into the historical community names Grand-Mère (831) and Shawinigan-Sud (791) — NAR restoring finer-grained pre-merger designations.
substantive: True name changes that neither a boundary reassignment nor an encoding artefact explains. Quebec leads (611), then Nova Scotia (295) and Ontario (226) — a flatter geography than the boundary group, which is what you expect from one-off local corrections rather than a regional merger.

The texture is small and specific — delivery-area splits and consolidations (Glovertown → Glovertown South; Pomquet → Antigonish), not civic renamings in the news sense. This is the group most worth a manual spot-check each cycle: a genuine town renaming would hide here.
encoding: Not real changes. Between releases the feed's character encoding shifted, so accented French/Acadian names stored as mojibake were repaired to a clean form. 301 distinct names were fixed across 75,001 codes.

The count is dominated by the largest cities, because they sit on the most codes: Montréal alone is 20,184, Québec 18,891, Trois-Rivières 5,879, Lévis 5,362. Provincially that means Quebec (70,919) with a tail in Acadian New Brunswick and Ontario's Franco names (Orléans).

We surface the count for transparency but never mix it into any real-change total. Treating these as “renames” is exactly the trap that made the raw dataset read as 163,167 city changes when only ~12,074 are genuine.
